# Hardening Tests — Deep Context

## Purpose
This module is the executable specification for the shell/orchestrator layer. It locks down subprocess tool permissions, JSON streaming expectations, timeout safety, content validation, install behavior, stale-context recovery, Codex integration, CLI entrypoint behavior, and ignore-rule precedence.

## Files In Scope
- `tests/hardening/t1-tool-lockdown.sh`
- `tests/hardening/t2-stream-filter.sh`
- `tests/hardening/t3-content-validation.sh`
- `tests/hardening/t4-timeouts-pipe-guards.sh`
- `tests/hardening/t5-portability-install.sh`
- `tests/hardening/t6-auto-mode.sh`
- `tests/hardening/t7-cli-entrypoint.sh`
- `tests/hardening/t7-codex-auto-mode.sh`
- `tests/hardening/t8-ignore-rules.sh`

## Core Responsibilities
- Assert required shell flags and allowed-tools restrictions.
- Assert `jq` and stream-json handling exist.
- Reject stubbed or malformed `.context/` and report artifacts.
- Assert timeout wrappers, pipe guards, and clear failures for malformed meta.
- Assert install scripts copy shared runtime assets and stale project scripts get refreshed.
- Mock agent CLIs to test end-to-end recovery/consolidation behavior without real LLM work.
- Assert `.edcignore` vs `--ignore` semantics.

## Invariants and Assumptions
- Runtime strings/flags are part of the compatibility contract.
- The checked-in `scripts/edc-review.sh` file is a supported artifact, not just an install output.
- Mocked-agent tests rely on prompt markers like `edc-build`, `edc-update`, or task-file phrasing staying stable.

## Trust Boundaries
- Tests use temporary repos and fake binaries; they assume runtime code remains hermetic enough to exercise in isolation.
- Some tests are intentionally static/grep-based and therefore couple to exact strings.

## Cross-Module Coupling
- Most tightly coupled to `runtime-cli` and `plugin-surface`.
- Also asserts expectations about installer output locations and agent-wrapper behavior.

## Fragility and Issues
- Test logic intentionally duplicates some runtime knowledge (paths, flags, prompt markers). That catches regressions early, but renames/refactors in the runtime layer carry high test-update cost.

# hardening-tests - Deep Context

## Purpose

This module is the repository's contract suite. It validates that the wrapper/orchestrator pipeline stays safe, visible, portable, and self-driving across supported runtime paths.

## Files

- `tests/hardening/t1-tool-lockdown.sh`
- `tests/hardening/t2-stream-filter.sh`
- `tests/hardening/t3-content-validation.sh`
- `tests/hardening/t4-timeouts-pipe-guards.sh`
- `tests/hardening/t5-portability-install.sh`
- `tests/hardening/t6-auto-mode.sh`
- `tests/hardening/t7-cli-entrypoint.sh`
- `tests/hardening/t7-codex-auto-mode.sh`
- `tests/hardening/t8-ignore-rules.sh`

## Coverage Map

- Tool lockdown and stream visibility.
- Stub-fraud rejection for context/review outputs.
- Timeout fallback correctness and malformed-meta handling.
- Portability and install behavior.
- End-to-end auto-mode orchestration with mocked Claude/Codex runtimes.
- CLI wrapper argument forwarding.
- Ignore-rule precedence.

## Invariants They Pin

- Every `claude -p` invocation stays tool-locked.
- Stream-json output stays visible through the filter.
- Missing/stub headings are fatal for context and report validation.
- Timeouts remain configurable and consistently wrapped.
- Runtime wrappers preserve expected flags and prompt text.
- Ignore rules never accidentally review EDC's own scratch outputs.

## Assumptions

- Shell-level tests are acceptable for workflow contracts that cross process boundaries.
- Exact strings are part of the public contract, not incidental implementation details.

## Issues / Fragility

- The tests are intentionally implementation-aware, so benign refactors can trigger broad updates.
- The Node hook path receives less direct regression coverage than the shell pipeline.
